cur:manuscripts-sacramentary-charles-bal.summary: The letter T of the 'Te igitur' prayer is formed by the cross, on which Christ hangs with outstretched arms, his head inclined and his body modelled in warm flesh tones, wearing a loincloth; busts of the Sun and Moon appear in medallions above the cross-arm, and a serpent coils at its foot. Lush acanthus and interlace fill the purple-and-gold page around him.
facts: The fragment of this sacramentary has five full-page miniatures and two initial pages; the Crucifixion forms the initial of the Canon of the Mass.
The serpent at the foot of the cross recalls the defeat of the serpent of Eden by Christ's death.
cur:manuscripts-sacramentary-charles-bal.notes: Folio not given on the Commons file (likely 6v). Attribution of this file to Latin 1141 follows its Commons category.

vam:O92636.summary: In the top register the Virgin lies on her deathbed surrounded by the apostles, St Peter swinging a censer and St Paul at the foot of the bed, while Christ stands behind the bier holding up a small figure of her soul, and angels descend to receive it. Below stand saints in two rows — Gregory of Nyssa and Basil, Peter and Paul embracing, and Cosmas and Damian, Nicholas and John Chrysostom — each identified by inscription. The plaque once formed the centre of a Byzantine triptych.
facts: The V&A places it in the so-called 'Nikephoros group' of Byzantine ivories, named after the panel on the Cortona reliquary of the True Cross associated by inscription with the Emperor Nikephoros II Phokas.
As frequently on Byzantine ivories, the back is carved with a large cross, here with rosettes at the ends of its arms.
The figure of the Virgin's soul held by Christ is a restoration (V&A).

links.label: Wikipedia: Dormition of the Mother of God

vam:O92636.notes: Byzantine (Constantinople), late 10th or early 11th century. The Dormition is not narrated in Scripture, so no passage is given. Formerly in the Webb collection, acquired 1867.

walters:W.42.62R.summary: In the bowl of a blue initial Q, the haloed Christ, book in hand, raises his right hand in a commanding gesture against a hairy, red-faced devil who shrinks back beside him. The initial begins Psalm 51 (52), 'Quid gloriaris in malitia' ('Why do you boast in malice?'), and the painter answers the psalm's boaster with the image of Christ's authority over evil. The lively little scene sits at the foot of a page framed by gold, blue and red penwork.
facts: Psalm 51 ('Quid gloriaris') was one of the standard divisions of the Gothic Psalter; the Walters lists it among the eight surviving historiated initials in this book.
The Psalter was produced for Jernoul de Camphaing, named in a red inscription on fol. 226r, in the third quarter of the 13th century.
Later owners added a small group of suffrages on originally blank leaves at the end in the 14th century, a sign of continued use.

links.label: The Digital Walters: Psalter of Jernoul de Camphaing (W.42)

walters:W.42.62R.notes: The Walters TEI calls this an initial 'D', but the image and text show the Q of 'Quid gloriaris' (the online title's 'Initial Q' is correct). Worklist year 750 was a parsing error.

feat:roerich-signs-of-christ.summary: Among wind-rippled dunes of ochre sand beneath blue hills, a long-haired figure of Christ sits tracing mysterious signs in the sand with a staff, while a hooded companion bends over him to watch. Roerich, the Russian painter, mystic and explorer, was fascinated by legends of Christ's presence in Asia and painted him as a quiet wanderer in a timeless landscape. The flat, glowing colours give the scene the stillness of an icon.
facts: The painting belongs to Roerich's 'Banners of the East' series, which portrays teachers and prophets of many religions.
It was painted in 1924 in Darjeeling, where the Roerich family had settled after arriving in India; the canvas, in tempera, measures about 74 by 118 cm.
In 1925, during his Central Asian expedition, Roerich recorded legends in Ladakh about 'Issa' (Jesus) travelling in India, which he retold in his book Altai–Himalaya.

commons:144223450.summary: A towering white marble Christ stands on the hill of Casablanca, his right hand raised in blessing and his left on his heart, looking across the bay toward old Havana. The Cuban sculptor Jilma Madera carved the figure from Carrara marble in Italy, and it was assembled on site from 67 blocks, which had been blessed by Pope Pius XII before shipping. It was unveiled at Christmas 1958, just days before the Cuban Revolution triumphed.
facts: The statue was inaugurated on 24 December 1958; on 1 January 1959 Fulgencio Batista fled Cuba, and on 8 January Fidel Castro entered Havana.
The project is often said to have been promoted by Marta Fernández Miranda, wife of President Batista, in fulfilment of a vow.
Madera won the commission in 1953; the statue is about 20 metres tall including its 3-metre base and weighs roughly 320 tonnes.
